catalog_quote: ... In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs. 2b. Stress Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable of a word or phrase in MANGBETU, accompanied sometimes by extra high tone as in nɛkâ- ‘kídriɔ, headache. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA’DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words, even when it is a vowel Prefix, e.g. 'iza, meat; after a consonant ...

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. the copy consulted contains the passage exactly as the report quotes it. I re-queried Open Library search-inside independently (raw response. overlapping highlights in, both in the mang1394 folder, appended). The phrase "Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable" returns exactly one hit in the whole IA full-text index: item linguisticanalys0000tuck = Tucker & Bryan 1966, Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa. Overlapping snippets reproduce the whole chain: "..MORU-MANGBETU LANGUAGES 31 / Falling and Rising tones are found only in MANGBETU-MEJE.. In all these languages there are Tone Classes in Nou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mangbetu is a tone language (H, L plus falling/rising contours per Demolin 1991); on top of tone, Larochette (as reported by Tucker & Bryan) observed a tendency for stress to fall on the penultimate syllable of the word or phrase, sometimes accompanied by extra-high pitch. Hyman 1977 and Ruhlen 1975/76 (via Downing 2004: 111) accordingly list Mangbetu as 'dominant penultimate stress (as well as tone)'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported in the accessible passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Described only as a 'tendency'; no exceptions given in the snippet. The scanned example 'neka-*kidri' (headache) has uncertain diacritics.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain explicitly 'word or phrase' — the penultimate prominence may be phrase-level (utterance-penult) rather than strictly lexical word stress; statement is second-hand (Tucker & Bryan summarising Larochette 1958) and was read only through search snippets, not a held scan. Demolin's first-hand 1991 phonology sketch (held) describes tone and syllable structure but says nothing about stress. Alternative coding: tone language with a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's stress remark is attributed to 'MANGBETU' specifically (Larochette's Mangbetu proper = Glottolog Nuclear Mangbetu nucl1420), as distinct from 'MANGBETU-MEJE' used elsewhere in their chapter; Larochette 1958 and Vekens 1928 also cover Medje/Meje (meje1239) and Makere (make1250), all dialects of mang1394. Demolin 1991/1992 describe Mangbetu proper (nord-est Zaïre, Uele). Hartell 1993 and McKee's SIL work concern the Meje dialect.

new_statements.quote: [p. 10, ACCENTS] Il y a trois accents : L'accent de quantité indiquant que la voyelle doit être allongée. [...] L'accent musical fait élever le son de la voix. L'accent tonique, ou ictus, appuie sur une ou plusiers [sic] syllabes d'un mot. [...] Nous avons dû renoncer à imprimer le signe de l'accent musical (~) et celui de l'accent tonique (´). [p. 25] Les formes de la première et de la troisième personne [...] se distinguent par l'accent tonique, c'est-à-dire qu'à la troisième personne on appuie sur la première syllabe. [p. 43] l'absence d'accent tonique sur la première syllabe indiquera le conditionnel tandis que l'accent tonique bien marqué indiquera le mode indicatif.
new_statements.translation: [p. 10] There are three accents: the accent of quantity, indicating that the vowel must be lengthened. [...] The musical accent raises the pitch of the voice. The tonic accent, or ictus, bears on one or several syllables of a word. [...] We have had to give up printing the sign of the musical accent (~) and that of the tonic accent (´). [p. 25] The first- and third-person forms [of the possessive] ... are distinguished by the tonic accent, i.e. in the third person one stresses the first syllable. [p. 43] the absence of tonic accent on the first syllable will indicate the conditional, whereas a well-marked tonic accent will indicate the indicative mood.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' record (Tucker & Bryan 1966 < Larochette 1958: tone classes; tendency to penultimate stress). Vekens independently (30 years earlier) attests both distinctive pitch and an 'accent tonique ou an earlier reading' in Mangbetu, and adds that stress can carry grammatical contrasts (first-syllable stress for 3rd-person possessives and for indicative vs conditional). He does NOT state a default penultimate (or any fixed) position, so he neither confirms nor denies Larochette's penult tendency; his two positional remarks concern the first syllable but as morphological markers (and in disyllabic andra/andre first = penult), not as a general rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Vekens distinguishes three prosodic 'accents' in Mangbetu: vowel length (marked with a circumflex), a 'musical accent' = raised pitch (tone, which he says distinguishes singular from plural of nouns and adjectives and several tense/person forms), and an 'accent tonique ou an earlier reading' = stress, which 'bears on one or several syllables of a word'. He gives no default position for the stress; the stress and pitch marks were left unprinted. The only positional statements are grammatical: 3rd-person possessive forms (andra/andre/andro 'son') are stressed on the first syllable unlike the homographic 1st-person forms, and in the 'passé indéfini plus éloigné' a well-marked stress on the first syllable signals the indicative, its absence the past conditional. So: a language with distinctive pitch (tone) plus a word stress that is not described as fixed and carries some grammatical contrasts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described as such; the an earlier reading is said to fall on 'one or several syllables of a word' (p. 10), without ranking.
new_statements.exceptions: Grammatical uses of stress: first-syllable stress marks 3rd- vs 1st-person possessives (p. 25) and indicative vs past conditional (p. 43). Pitch ('accent musical / de hauteur') is separately contrastive: noun plural formed 'en modifiant l'accent musical' with no constant rule (p. 15-16), adjective number (p. 22), sg. vs pl. persons (p. 44 n.7), remote future vs remote past on -bu (p. 47 n.5), -ba (p. 48 n.6), ka 'déjà' vs ka 'ne pas' (p. 92); questions marked only by the voice rising on the first syllable (p. 61). Author notes Medje/Makere differ from Mangbetu only in dialectal particulars.
new_statements.identity_note: Vekens describes 'l'idiome mangbetu' proper as spoken around Rungu/Niangara (Haut-Uele), the lingua franca of the Mangbetu chiefdoms, noting that Medje and Makere speech differs only by dialectal particulars he flags in passing (e.g. p. 66-67); all three fall under Glottolog mang1394 Mangbetu (Meje and Makere are its dialects).

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. The catalog (via Tucker & Bryan 1966 reporting Larochette 1958) records tone classes plus a tendency to penultimate stress in Mangbetu; Vekens 1928 confirms the coexistence of distinctive pitch ('accent musical') and stress ('accent tonique ou an earlier reading') but gives no default stress position, saying only that the an earlier reading falls on one or several syllables of a word and that first-syllable stress distinguishes 3rd-person possessives and the indicative from the past conditional. The penult tendency therefore rests on Larochette alone; Vekens is silent on it rather than opposed.
